speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. RENE TREMBLAY AND THE LATE MAURICE RINFRET EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET ON PASSING OF FORMER MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with deep dismay that I learned, as most members, of the death of Hon. Rene Tremblay which occurred just before noon today. We knew that he had been ill, but we expected that he would still be with us for a long time.
Mr. Tremblay had a rather brilliant career. He studied in Canada and in Europe. He was at first professor at Laval University and then became deputy minister of the department of industry and trade in Quebec. In 1963 he was elected member for Matapedia-Matane. Soon afterwards he was appointed Minister for Citizenship and Immigration-he was thus one of my predecessors-to become eventually Postmaster General.
Mr. Tremblay was not only our colleague, he was everyone's colleague and he was also a personal friend. We are of the same generation not only as far as age is concerned but also from a political standpoint.
You will understand, Mr. Speaker, that as other members of this house, we are particularly affected by this sudden demise, particularly when it is realized that it follows upon the death of Hon. Mr. Favreau and our friend, Maurice Rinfret. This might lead us to ponder on the effects on health of political tensions which may possibly be felt more particularly by the group to which I have the pleasure and the honour to belong.
The death of Hon. Rene Tremblay is surely a loss for the province of Quebec but it is also a loss for the whole country. I am sure that the members of this house will be unanimous in expressing to his wife and to his children their most sincere condolences.
Personally, I regret that, before leaving us, he did not have the good fortune of seeing certain injustices committed against him repaired as they should have been. But this is
probably what one can expect in politics; we are in a ring where the opponents do not always pull their blows and it is in circumstances such as those that we realize that we are mere human beings.
As I have already said, Mr. Speaker, to the name of Hon. Mr. Tremblay we must add that of another friend, a sincere friend of all, that of the hon. member for Saint-Jacques, Maurice Rinfret. He presided over the proceedings of the house with a great deal of humour, of kindness. I do believe that regardless of political affiliations everyone liked Maurice Rinfret. I think, therefore, that the house should also agree to express its condolences to Mrs. Rinfret.
Mr. Rinfret was ill for a very long time. He was seriously ill when he was last with us here, and yet he never complained and no one even noticed it.
At this moment of our political history, Mr. Speaker, when there are so many problems which we must face collectively, it is particularly painful to witness events such as these.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. RENE TREMBLAY AND THE LATE MAURICE RINFRET EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET ON PASSING OF FORMER MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself and the members of the official opposition with the comments of the minister regarding the late Maurice Rinfret and Hon. Mr. Tremblay.
I was shocked to learn during the recess of the death of Mr. Rinfret who served in this house as the member for Saint-Jacques and as Deputy Chairman of Committees. Although it was not my privilege to serve with him in the house for any length of time, I quickly became aware of the position of respect and esteem that he held among members of all parties in the House of Commons. I was not aware of his illness and it was a great shock to me when he passed away during the recess of the house. Certainly we would wish to extend our sympathies to Madame Rinfret and members of the family.
Mr. Tremblay, as the minister indicated, served his province and the country in both elective and non-elective offices, having been in the public service of the province of Quebec before he entered the House of Commons. He was educated in both official languages and his education spanned two continents. He
57G0	COMMONS
Tributes to Deceased Members attended Laval and McGill Universities and completed his education on the continent of Europe.
Although he resigned from the cabinet over two years ago he continued to take an active part in and make a positive contribution to political life in this country, particularly with regard to leading questions of our day concerning national unity and economic affairs, which he was particularly well qualified to discuss by reason of his background and education.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of the opposition I should like to extend my deepest sympathy to Mrs. Tremblay and her children, as well as to the members of the Liberal party.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. RENE TREMBLAY AND THE LATE MAURICE RINFRET EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET ON PASSING OF FORMER MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of this party I should like to join with those who have already spoken in expressing our very deep and sincere regret at the passing of two of our colleagues.
Mr. Ren6 Tremblay, who was for some time the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, we came to know very well. I can speak for members of this party in saying that we always found him accessible and courteous. He approached the problems of his department with a deep sense of humanity and with a fine compassion, which we greatly appreciated.
The passing of our colleague Maurice Rin-fret is also to be regretted, Mr. Speaker. Many of us came to know him quite well during his time in the house. Personally I had the privilege of being with a Speaker's delegation which visited the Soviet union and Czechoslovakia something over two years ago. We found him a delightful companion and a person who was deeply motivated for the welfare and benefit of this country.
We are exceedingly sorry at the passing of these two members of this house. We should like to extend, through you, Mr. Speaker, to their wives and families our deepest sympathy in their hour of bereavement.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of sitting with Hon. Mr. Tremblay on the committee on the national anthem of Canada and that is where I had the opportunity of realizing his good sense, his good judgment, the firmness of his decisions, as well as his deep convictions.

Mr. Speaker, as we think of our two colleagues who have been removed from our midst we share the sense of loss and the feelings of deep regret which have been expressed in the house this afternoon. Though we knew that Maurice Rinfret had been seriously ill, we hoped that he would return to the house and that he would be spared for a considerable time. It was a shock to hear that he had passed away.
It has been said that every member of the house held Mr. Rinfret in the deepest respect. I say that for many of us the feeling went beyond respect; we held him in affection, especially when we considered his qualities of character and the attitudes that he evidenced on many occasions.
We are reminded again of the shortness of life in the passing of Hon. Rene Tremblay, which was perhaps more unexpected than that of Mr. Rinfret.

speechtext: While joining, on behalf of all hon. members, in the words of regret we have just heard at the passing of Hon. Rene Tremblay, may I speak very briefly about the man who for two years was associated with the functions of Speaker of the house and Chairman of the Committees. A loyal colleague and a wise adviser, a faithful worker of the first hour and the last, Maurice Rinfret gave himself completely to his parliamentary responsibilities. subtopic: MR. WINTERS-ALLEGED INACCURACY IN NEWSPAPER REPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: MR. WINTERS-ALLEGED INACCURACY IN NEWSPAPER REPORT
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. On Friday, January 12, the Toronto Daily Star misquoted me in a headline as saying of the government that "it lacks integrity". Mr. Speaker, I said no such thing. In fact, I said nothing which could be considered as meaning that the government lacks integrity, fiscal or otherwise.
In replying to a question I said that whoever becomes the new leader must attach great importance to fiscal integrity-the fiscal soundness of the country as a whole. In this, of course, the role of the federal government is just one part of the national fiscal structure. I was speaking of the country, not of the government, and in any event I did not say anything which would justify the attribution to me of a quotation such as that which appeared in the newspaper.

subtopic: MR. WINTERS-ALLEGED INACCURACY IN NEWSPAPER REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Statement on Foreign Exchange FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief statement on the foreign exchange situation and table a press announcement made during the week end.
During the ten days preceding this week end there have been abnormally large sales of Canadian dollars in the foreign exchange markets, and we have had to meet these demands by sales of United States dollars from our reserves. This has been evident to those in the market and has been reported in the press.
This selling pressure resulted in part from widespread nervousness in international financial circles about currencies generally following the devaluation of sterling and the abnormal demands for gold. More immediately, however, it appears to have resulted in part from highly exaggerated fears of the effects on Canada of the United States balance of payments regulations, and misunderstanding of the intention of the United States authorities in that regard. In order to clarify this situation, we discussed it with the Secretary of the Treasury and his officers during the week end and they have issued a statement on the matter which has been reported in the press, and a copy of which I wish to table.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. minister permission to table this document?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On our side the Governor of the Bank of Canada, following discussions with the chartered banks, issued a statement last night saying it had been agreed that the banks would discourage the use of bank credit to facilitate abnormal transfers of funds abroad by Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies and would also discourage the use of bank credit by such companies to meet requirements in Canada which in the past have normally been met by parent companies. These discussions with the banks were undertaken by the governor after he and I had discussed the matter and agreed that such action was desirable.
The governor also increased the bank rate yesterday from 6 per cent to 7 per cent in the light of recent developments in the exchange market. He had consulted me as usual before taking this action. I believe this move was
5762	COMMONS
Statement on Foreign Exchange appropriate and prudent to protect the Canadian dollar against speculation and strengthen our position. I regret, as we all will regret, that external circumstances have made this step necessary.
Today the market situation has improved. The value of the Canadian dollar in the market has risen and we have bought some United States dollars to ensure that the market readjustment was an orderly one. It is of course too early to draw definite conclusions, but the change is distinctly encouraging.
Our present exchange parity is appropriate to our economic situation and should be and will be maintained. We have very large exchange and gold reserves to defend it, and we also have access to large supplementary sources of finance through the International Monetary Fund and through a reciprocal support arrangement between the Bank of Canada and the federal reserve system, which was increased last fall to $750 million. Our basic position is safeguarded by our unrestricted access to the long-term capital market of the United States, where Canada and Canadian borrowers enjoy high credit ratings. We are fully prepared, if this should be necessary, to use our reserves and the other resources available to us, to defend the Canadian dollar in the exchange markets.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a subject on which, of course, one must weigh his words with some care. I am pleased at the reassurance of the minister regarding the determination to maintain the value of our dollar. I am also pleased that he is able to report to the house that the initial results, at least, of the increase in the bank rate appear to be favourable, and certainly I know every member of the house hopes most fervently that these initial, apparently beneficial, results will continue and that nothing further will be required.
I am sure we all have a tremendous confidence in the future of our country, and it should be a matter for all of us who are responsible to make certain that we realize the potential of our country. However, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be inappropriate for me to say that the results in the country of the increase in the bank rate are not likely to be very desirable from a domestic point of view, and that consequently it is regrettable that the Governor of the Bank of Canada found it necessary to make this decision.

I emphasize that in the circumstances I am not criticizing his decision. I am quite prepared to accept his judgment in this regard. Nevertheless I think that this is a further indication of the importance of confidence in government or, if you like, in the country- confidence in our willingness and readiness to assure that our country will maintain its economic strength.
Just as I had occasion in the course of the so-called mini-budget debate to suggest that the Canadian people were being asked to pay higher taxes as a measure of trying to restore confidence in the government, I now think that the increase in the bank rate is a further price that the Canadian people will pay with regard to confidence in and credibility of the government.
I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to appear to be lecturing the government in any pedantic way, but I think it would be appropriate for me to remind members of the government that they have a heavy responsibility during coming months, or for at least as long as it remains their responsibility to form a government.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

I hope they will make every effort to demonstrate to all concerned that they are prepared to do what is necfessary to ensure the economic future, strength and stability of our country, because it is really a question of confidence. I hope the government will pursue policies and attitudes which will inspire confidence. As I take my seat I again repeat that I hope the measure that is taken by the Bank of Canada will have not only the initial result but the continuing results that are considered necessary in this situation.

Mr. Speaker, like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), I am well aware that this is a very delicate matter on which to speak and that one must weigh one's words very carefully, because the basis of the operation of a modern monetary system is confidence. I myself am very disturbed by the inevitable results of the action the government has taken, action which it was obliged to take because of its previous policy decisions about which I have spoken on previous
January 22. 1968	COMMONS
occasions; that is, the incompatible policies of the fixed exchange rate plus the agreement on exchange reserves which are continually coming in conflict.
1 am not at all sure that the people of Canada will be satisfied with the way in which the government and the Bank of Canada have dealt with this problem of protecting the Canadian dollar, because the Canadian people will have to suffer for it. There is no question but that the general level of interest rates will rise, that our already acute situation in respect of housing will become worse, that government financing will become more expensive and as a consequence our economy will slow down even more.
I would have hoped that in view of the critical situation in which we find ourselves the government would be prepared at this time to re-assess its whole policy with regard to our exchange rate and its whole policy with regard to our relations with the United States. I and some of my colleagues have suggested earlier in this house that the situation at the present time, even before this immediate crisis had arisen, called for rethinking in respect of our attitude with regard to the fixed exchange rate. It is demonstrated by the present economic problem in this country that we should go back to the floating interest rate and the control of the inflow and outflow of capital from Canada.
The government's present action seems again to be placing the burden on the ordinary Canadian citizen, because it has tied its hands with regard to the monetary and fiscal policy so that it is unable to cope with this problem without curbing the development of the Canadian economy in a way which, in the end, must fundamentally undermine our position internationally far more than any temporary attack on the Canadian dollar,- and which attack would be very severe if continued for any length of time.
I would again point out, as I did a few weeks ago in this house, that when we were on the floating exchange rate which lasted for 12 years the fluctuations were all within a very narrow range of 3 cents United States during that whole period. I would hope that somewhat the same situation would occur now. But in order to prevent anything more drastic in the way of upward pressure, which is equally as dangerous as downward 27053-364

Statement on Foreign Exchange pressure, I would suggest that the government consider the imposition of emergency exchange controls.

Mr. Speaker, I share the concern the minister has expressed in saying he regrets the external circumstances which exist that have made it necessary for the Bank of Canada to step up the interest rates, as it has done. I would just like to add that this serves as an additional reminder that the economic situation both within and outside the country is most serious at the present time. The policy of raising federal housing interest rates to the present level, instead of drawing more capital out of the private sector, has served only to push interest rates still higher. This action today will have the same effect. One wonders just how high interest rates can go.
I should like to remind the minister as he seeks to deal with these problems, many of which are outside his own direct control, that never since 1929 have we faced a problem of high interest rates such as that we have now, and that this action, which may have been necessary at the immediate moment, will serve only to increase further our financial problems. In this regard it relates also to the continued policy of those who control international monetary values in respect of gold being held at the present price. One wonders how long in the future it will be before the price of gold will have to be increased, its having held the same price it holds now while other commodities have doubled or even quadrupled in price.
We share the expression of regret the minister has made in his statement, but we hope he will use every possible effort to bring about some more permanent and more satisfactory solution to the problems of international liquidity and stability of our own dollar, and the problem of the continual rise in the cost of interest and the continued tight money policy which makes Canada's development so difficult.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the Canadian Meat and Canned Foods Act and regulations, meat must be prepared in establishments approved by the government and under the constant control of government veterinary inspectors.
However, section 68 of the regulations provides that the legend on meat inspected shall be marked in English only. This bill provides that the legend shall be bilingual and decorated with the maple leaf appearing on the Canadian flag.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

In recent years the problem has become somewhat more complex because of man made changes such as development of the world's fair site, and the presence of commercial shipping in the channel opened by icebreakers for flood control. In recognition of this the department last year initiated an intensive investigation of ice problems, including an expanded program of systematic data collection and observance of ice conditions. As an additional ice control measure, dredged material is being used to construct several artificial islands in the general area of the ice booms. speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Yes, (a) selected members of the Canadian forces of all ranks are now using the
January 22, 1968

proposed new salute; (b) the proposed salute is effected as follows:
(1) To salute to the front, bend the right elbow and bring the right hand by the shortest route to the position at the headdress. (2) During the movement, the back of the hand is uppermost with the fingers together and straight. Continue the upward movement with the palm of the hand down. In the position of the salute, the fingers are extended, together, with the tip of the forefinger approximately in line with the right eyebrow, the upper arm (from shoulder to elbow) horizontal. The forearm, wrist and fingers are straight from the elbow to the point where the forefinger touches the cap. subtopic: DISCONTINUATION OF RURAL MAIL DELIVERIES ON SATURDAYS
speechtext:
1. Preliminary studies concerning the curtailment of postal service on weekends have been initiated. These studies are in line with recommendations 58 and 59 of the royal commission on working conditions in the Post Office Department.
Studies to date have dealt with the effect these recommendations would have on staff needs. Studies are under way to assess the full impact of the recommendations on such problems as storage space, delays to mail and other related considerations. There is also the question of public reaction to be resolved.
Only after a detailed analysis has been made of all factors concerned will it be possible to make concrete proposals as to the course of action, if any, that will be taken with regard to the curtailment of urban mail deliveries on Saturdays.
2. Any possible effect that a curtailment in postal services upon the weekends might have on rural mail delivery will be thoroughly examined.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Thursday, December 21, clause 2 of the bill was under consideration together with an amendment thereto proposed by the hon. member for Lapointe.
On clause 2-Broadcasting policy for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, shortly before the house recessed for Christmas on December 211 was making some remarks about this proposed legislation. Since then the leadership contest has, of course, been resolved- not the leadership contest within the government but the contest for the leadership of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-with the appointment last week of Dr. Davidson and Mr. Picard as the chief executive and operating officers of the corporation. I am sure all of us who took part in the events leading up to the introduction of this proposed legislation into this chamber, as well as all who served on the broadcasting committee and are interested in broadcasting even in a peripheral way, wish the new officers every success in what will be a difficult and responsible task, especially in the context of the constitutional situation we are experiencing at this time.
I realize I have only about two minutes of my speaking time remaining at this stage in the examination of the bill. In my remarks on December 21 I drew attention to a number of provisions in the bill with which I did not find myself completely in agreement, weaknesses which I hoped could be corrected in the course of our clause by clause study. In the seconds remaining to me I should like to
January 22, 1968

say there are other areas in the bill which leave me in a state of anxiety.
My criticisms and comments of December 21 did not express my point of view completely. For example, I am not happy about the provision which authorizes a five-year capital budget for the corporation, though I believe a period longer than one year would be valuable. I realize that the new officers would have to operate under severe restrictions if they were obliged to return year after year for approval of their capital budget, and I believe they deserve more than one year of leeway in this regard. Nevertheless I am not happy about the five year provision and it seems to me an acceptable compromise could be worked out that would be satisfactory both to the officials of the corporation and to those of us here who must try to exercise control over the affairs of the C.B.C. The Secretary of State can contradict the hon. member for Lotbiniere because she was a member of the cabinet of the present government when it became necessary to pass exceptive legislation through a special order in council to legalize the operations of the two private stations in Quebec city. Why was this necessary? Simply and only because they contravened the previous broadcasting act which stipulated that the majority stockholders in a private television station must be Canadian citizens. The Secretary of State knows that. In order to progress more rapidly, the Secretary of State has only to put the record straight and tell the hon. member for Lotbiniere that he is wrong; nothing more. I hope that the hon. member for Lotbiniere will admit at least that he is wrong since the cabinet, the Prime Minister, the then Secretary of State and the then Minister of Transport had to introduce and pass a special order in council in 1965 to legalize that situation.
I put the question on the order paper, and tonight at eight o'clock I will answer the hon. member for Lotbiniere. He will see then that an order in council was issued, not only for the private Quebec station, but for five private radio and television stations throughout Canada. Exceptive legislation was passed concerning five private stations, and the two private Quebec stations were among those five. A special order in council was issued because these stations did not conform to the law stipulating that these radio and television stations had to be Canadian-owned.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere should apologize and correct the mistake he made earlier. I realize that he cannot know everything. But that does not mean I accuse the directors of the two private Quebec stations. That is false.
Would the hon. member allow me a question?

If the hon. member is only asking questions, as he said earlier, to tease me, well I think that the house has no time to waste. If it is a serious question, that is fine,
January 22, 1968

but if it has to do with the father of somebody or the father of a producer on channel 4, I could not care less. Such things do not matter; only the principle is important.

Could I ask the hon.
member a question? Does he know that I have been advised that channel 4 is controlled by Canadian interests and that its programs are truly representative of Quebec? Does the hon. member know that? If not, I will tell him so.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Lotbiniere has some information which is not available to us, I would be pleased to obtain it. If, at the present time, channel 4 is owned by Canadian interests, I should be very happy. However, I have in hand the figures which were supplied to us by the hon. Secretary of State.
Secondly, the cabinet passed an order in council to legalize the situation of channel 4.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere says that the ownership is 50 per cent American and 50 per cent Canadian when the figures say this: 51.8 per cent American and 48.2 per cent Canadian. We say fifty-fifty in round figures: 133 Liberals, 132 Conservatives, 50-50 no prime minister. It is simple as that.
On the other hand, if the hon. member for Lotbiniere tells me that he knows that, that he has other statistics, I am prepared to resume my seat and to have him give us those figures. Would the hon. member for Lotbiniere have figures other than those we were given by the hon. Secretary of State? The hon. member for Lotbiniere has often put questions to me; I, in turn, ask him if he has figures other than those which were supplied to me by the hon. Secretary of State.

Mr. Chairman, it is certainly unfair to discuss in this way. The hon. member admits himself that he cannot prove that there is American influence on channel 4. He quotes figures, and I have mine. I know clearly that 75 per cent of channel 4 belongs to Canadian interests. I know clearly that all the programs on channel 4 are Quebec programs. I would suggest to the hon. member that he take a walk on the Champs-Elysees in Paris; he would see that there are many theatres where American films translated into French are shown. This is not detrimental to French culture. Let the hon. member be serious once and for all and let him stop bringing charges indiscriminately. He has been repeating the same thing for about three hours.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting

Order.
I am sorry to interrupt the debate but the hon. member is out of order since the amendment before the committee at the present time says: "that the television stations shall be controlled by Canadians" but not necessarily the number of shares of each company.
speakername: @Deputy Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speechtext: Could we now vote on the amendment?

As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, it is not a question of shares, but of control, as it is said in the bill. I am satisfied with the legislation as it stands; as a matter of fact, clause 2 (b) which I seek to have amended, says here, in part:
the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians

There is no mention there of the number of shares, but it is stated that it should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians, in a proportion of 52, 53 or 51 per cent. The moment Canadians have 51 per cent, they own, they control effectively.
I am glad, Mr. Chairman, that you reminded us that the hon. member was out of order, because he would have drawn me in an altogether different field. You understand, I am sure, that when the hon. member for Lotbiniere talks about Mr. Adrien Pouliot who is responsible for the opening of French C.B.C. stations in the West, twenty-five years ago, I agree with him, but he leads me astray.
Therefore, I revert to my topic, hoping that the hon. member for Lotbiniere will not lead me further off the track.
I say it is fine, because it was provided for by the words "should be owned". But what happened is that the cabinet passed orders in council and exceptive measures to legalize the situation of television stations not owned and controlled effectively by Canadians. The Quebec station is one of those and is being operated under an order in council. The Secretary of State cannot deny it, because she is the one who gave that reply herself in answer to a question I put last fall. If the situation has changed, let the Secretary of State say so right now and I shall take her word for it, but that was the situation less than three months ago when that television station was being operated under an order in council. So I submit that instead of saying "should", which allows exceptive legislation and orders in council enabling Americans-in this case Famous Players-to control the Quebec station, we should say "shall"; it would then become
5812	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the law. What does "should" mean? It made possible all the exceptions we have had in the past and that is what we are trying to avoid. We do not want any exceptions. We want it to be as when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) took his responsibilities. At one time, he said that all chartered operating in Canada had to be owned by Canadian residents and citizens in a proportion of 75 per cent of the common shares and voting shares. He had the legislation enacted and did not write in it "should" but "shall" and there are no exceptions. He can grant them a delay to sell some of their shares. In the case of Famous Players, it does not mean that the directors would require to sell the whole television station; they could sell 2 or 3 per cent of the shares and it would solve the problem. It is as simple as that and that is what we are asking for. Perhaps the Secretary of State would be ready to accept that?
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with considerable interest to the discussion between the two hon. members, particularly since the hon. member for Lapointe seems to be talking about ownership by Quebecois and not by Canadians. This is, of course, a considerably different issue and one with which the legislation does not deal at all.

Would the hon. minister allow me to speak?

In my amendment, I did not suggest that the words "effectively controlled and owned by Canadians" should be changed. I did not alter those words. I merely asked that the word "should" replaced the word "must" and I did not ask at all that the word "Canadians" be deleted. As long as we are part of the Confederation, Mr. Chairman, and I have always said so, I will accept the standards of the country and I will consider myself a Canadian citizen. We are still members of the Confederation, that is true, but when we no longer belong to it, the word Quebecker will apply. I did not ask that the word be changed, I only asked the substitution of "must" for "should". I hope that the Secretary of State will accept it.

I am glad my hon. friend did not because he would have found himself in the minority, had he proposed that, not only in this chamber but probably in the

DEBATES	January 22. 1968
country. There was another piece of information for which my hon. friend asked which relates to the sheet of paper he has before him. I provided him with that some weeks ago and it relates to channels four and five in the city of Quebec. I do not have the opportunity to watch or listen to those channels but I have been told by my friend, the hon. member for Quebec East, that he has had the opportunity in the last 15 days to watch them almost nightly. Almost all of the programs to which he has listened have emanated from a European country, not from either Canada or the United States. These are obviously not programs which were manufactured or owned by the Famous Players Corporation of the United States.
The other information asked for by the hon. member is in respect of other Quebec radio and television stations. I must confess at once to a very serious lapse. I did not remember where I had obtained the information which I provided my hon. friend and which has formed the basis of the stimulating conversation of the last hour and the basis of the stimulating but perhaps not so acceptable charges against the operators of Quebec radio and television stations.
The hon. member wanted me to spend the period from six to eight o'clock industriously calling upon members of the B.B.G. to scurry down to the office and dig up information for me to produce at eight o'clock in order that the debate would not be held up. He suggested alternatively that the debate be held up until some time tomorrow so I could produce this information. Perhaps he will forgive me if I do not do that this evening between six and eight but instead advise him, and I appreciate that advice from a woman is never well received, particularly when publicly given, to go to the returns branch and ask for the return to the motion for the production of papers No. 122, which was tabled in the House of Commons on May 4, 1966 by the then minister of transport, Mr. Pickersgill. I am sure the hon. member will find that the sheet he has before him is one of the sheets of that particular tabled document and all the other sheets, which have been a matter of public knowledge now for almost two years by virtue of being in the public annals of the house, will be laid bare before his eyes and when we return at eight o'clock he will have enough further material for another hour's speech. May I call it six o'clock?
January 22, 1968
It being six o'clock it is my duty to leave the chair in order that the house may consider private members' business.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. House again in committee on Bill No. C-163, an act to implement a broadcasting policy for Canada.
On clause 2-Broadcasting Policy for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, as we rose at six o'clock a number of questions were put by the hon. member for Lapointe and, I suppose, a challenge was hurled at me to support the position taken by the hon. member for Lapointe with respect to the television stations CFCM-TV and CKMI-TV in Quebec city. It is not my function to support private broadcasting stations. Indeed, as all hon. members know, my function is to report to parliament on broadcasting in general. Normally I am not expected to take up the cudgels for any station, whether it be private or public. However, because of a number of things which were said by the hon. member for Lapointe in December, and again now, I did check on some information which I had received as a result of his earlier speech. I have to inform the house of these facts which, to the best of my knowledge and information, are correct and which are vouched for by Mr. Pouliot, the manager of that station who is a good Canadian. I am told that these two stations which are owned and operated by a Canadian company, namely Television-Quebec-Canada Ltee, are not owned in any way by United States subjects.
I am informed that not one share of that company is owned by a United States subject. In fact, my information is that 50 per cent of the shares of Television de Quebec are owned by Quebec companies or individuals, and these Quebeckers are still, and proudly so, Canadians, whether they be corporate or private. The other 50 per cent of the corporation is owned by Famous Players Canadian Corporation Limited which I am told is a Canadian company incorporated under the laws of Canada. Of its shares, 51 per cent are owned by United States subjects or companies, but that is of course not 51 per cent with respect to Television de Quebec.
January 22, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Furthermore, my information is that when in 1954 a licence was granted for CFCM-TV it was under the express condition that control of the company would not fall into the hands of Famous Players Canadian Corporation Limited. I am informed that the structure of Television de Quebec is such that Famous Players cannot have more than 50 per cent of the shares, and effective control is and must remain in the hands of Quebeckers. The president of Television de Quebec is a Canadian and a Quebecker, and so is the managing director. I am further informed that the managing director has the final say in matters of management, including approval of editorial matters.
I do not propose to interpose myself between the hon. member for Lapointe and Television de Quebec in what appears to be a strenuous difference of opinion over editorial content of that television station's program. I am informed that the public affairs programming has been many times under scrutiny by the B.B.G. and has been commended as being particularly Canadian.
I am further informed by Television de Quebec that their editorial policy favours freedom as against communism, private enterprise as against socialism and Canadian unity as against separatism. It may be because Television de Quebec is in the heart of a province which my hon. friend seeks to take out of the confederation of Canada, that he has lodged his complaint. But if my information is correct-and I would not place it before the house if I did not have every reason to believe it was correct-then I think that the hon. member should not attempt to mislead members of the house by indicating that this corporation and these stations are in any way under United States control.
Well said.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased with the explanations given to us by the hon. Secretary of State, except that when she refers to the policy followed by the private Quebec television stations in their programming, their editorials, or this or that orientation I must tell the hon. Secretary of State, that I did not introduce this matter in the conversation. The one who slipped the subject of the policies, or ideologies or editorials of the Quebec television stations, into our debate is the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who threw into that debate an allusion to an editorial that the


Quebec television station has reportedly written against me and which I have never heard of and never seen and which has quite failed to impress me.
Therefore, the hon. Secretary of State should not raise this argument: I did not raise the problem of the political ideology of the Quebec television station. It was raised by the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I should also correct the impression some people may have got, of whom, Mr. Adrien Pouliot, father of the general manager. I never introduced that into the debate. Because I speak of channel 4 in Quebec city, all of a sudden, the hon. member for Lotbiniere rises and intervenes saying: You don't speak against channel 4 in Quebec city, because its manager is Mr. Jean Pouliot, son of Mr. Adrien Pouliot who, years ago, contributed to the setting up of C.B.C. French stations out west.
I am not the one who introduced that in the debate. I have nothing against Mr. Adrien Pouliot; far from it, for I know him very well, perhaps even better than the hon. member for Lotbiniere. I have often met him. I have eaten with him and I admire him very much; he has contributed tremendously to French radio out west. But why bring this up? Why take the Quebec station to task? The general manager is the son of Mr. Adrien Pouliot who 15 years ago was a member of the Board of Governors of the C.B.C. I do not know who is the grandfather of the second cameraman of channel 4 in Quebec but it does not matter.
The Secretary of State mentions the editorials of the Quebec station. I have never mentioned them. I am not the one who brought this up in discussion, it was the member for Lotbiniere. I am not at all concerned with the editorials of the Quebec station. They are entitled to their opinions, it is freedom of thought, freedom of speech, freedom of the press. That I believe in, and I would not blame them for this.
Now when the Secretary of State tells me that the whole editorial policy is under the president of the Quebec station, she is saying that the president runs everything. But the president, Mr. Gaston Pratte, owns one out of 10,000 shares. Possibly, it is the vice-president Mr. J. J. Fitzgibbons, but he has also one share out of 10,000. Now, as far as the treasurer is concerned, Mr. Boldstad-I do not know where he comes from-but he owns only one share out of 10,000. It may be the secretary, Mr. Henri Lepage-whom I know
*January 22, 1968

too as a very good guy. I have nothing against him as secretary of the company-but he too, owns only one share out of 10,000.

Mr. Chairman, would my hon. friend permit a question? I apologize for asking it in English. Does my hon. friend recall the debate on December 20 last to which he made a very valuable contribution, beginning at page 5679 of Hansard, and does he remember saying this, as reported at the bottom of page 5680:
In Quebec, the only two private television stations are owned by American subjects. The result is that those two television stations present regularly news commentaries, three times a day on the French station and three times a day on the English station, and they are identical commentaries, translated back into English, since those two stations are owned by the same American company. When comments are made on a decision taken by the federal government or by the Quebec government or by a municipality, it is always the American point of view which is put forward during the news commentaries of those two Quebec stations, either the English or the French station. It is always the American point of view on, or reaction to, the events occurring in Canada and Quebeckers, as a result, are overwhelmed by American reactions.
That's a shame.

Mr. Chairman, this is precisely what I said because I submit that, according to the statistics provided by the Secretary of State, according to the order in council passed in 1965, the two private television stations in Quebec belong to American interests.
The Secretary of State claims that is not the case. So I would ask her why did the cabinet, the 25 ministers and the Prime Minister, and everybody, pass an order in council in 1965 making it legal through exceptive legislation to operate two private television stations in Quebec contrary to legislation providing that a majority of shares in a Canadian television station had to be in the hands of Canadian citizens. If the majority of shares were owned by Canadians, why did the cabinet bother to pass an order in council to make the situation legal and in accordance with the act?
That is the answer the Secretary of State gave me in October or November 1967, in reply to a question I had placed on the order paper. If things have changed in the last two or three months, let the Secretary of State tell me and I shall sit down. But we have not been notified of any changes, the order in
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting council has not been rescinded and so far the two Quebec private stations are still in operation under that order in council. Has the minister been bothered for nothing or what? Perhaps the Secretary of State could tell me what the situation is concerning that order in council?

Mr. Chairman, I would be happy to answer my hon. friend. He said that he did not deal with editorials and was not concerned with them. I ask him if he also remembers this passage, which is to be found on page 5680, the right-hand column, the same date, December 20. The hon. member said:
There is a young squirt who reads these editorials, possibly with some assurance, but everyone knows that he is not writing them;-
What page is that?
Page 5680.
Which column?

The right-hand column.
There is a young squirt who reads these editorials-
The hon. member is there referring to editorials which are prepared according to United States ideas and reactions of stations belonging to United States citizens.
-possibly with some assurance, but everyone knows that he is not writing them; nevertheless, they are regularly given over the Quebec television, either on the French station or on the English station.
Then my hon. friend goes on to indicate that he believes the former legislation, which must be the 1958 legislation, stated that television and radio stations in Canada "should belong to Canadians." Today my hon. friend has been talking about 50 per cent ownership. I would refer my hon. friend to the provisions of the 1958 act and particularly to section 14 (1) which required, and at the moment still does, licencees to have 75 per cent Canadian shareholders. The 1958 act provides under section 14 (2) for an exemption if there is less than 75 per cent.
Accordingly, these stations were granted the exemption under section 14 (2). But that does not mean-and my hon. friend has been using the word "majority", or at least that is the word the translators have been using -that more than 50 per cent is owned even by a United States corporation, much less that the ownership is comprised completely of
January 22, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting United States citizens. I think my hon. friend has perhaps been misled by a too careless reading of the legislation or perhaps by an understanding of it without actually checking the language. It seems clear that in the 1958 act the requirement was that at least 75 per cent be Canadian unless there be an exemption. This not being the case here, there being only 50 per cent Canadian and 50 per cent United States, it appears that management decisions are made for Canadians by Canadians, and in this case there was an exemption.
I am sure my hon. friend would want the record to be set straight because I have noticed in the years I have been in the house that he is a man of very generous propensities and would want to be very fair to a corporation that has no other way than this of making its voice heard on the floor of the house.
You are very generous.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with everything the Secretary of State has just said. What I have been trying to explain from the beginning, however, is that the present act can be very easily evaded. I put a question on the order paper last September asking how television stations were exempted by order in council from complying with section 14(1) just mentioned by the minister. She answered then that five television stations were exempted, including two in Quebec. Under the former act, television stations had to be owned by a clear majority of Canadian citizens. Why? Because wave lengths are public property and their number is restricted. It is not like a newspaper. When someone wants to found a newspaper, all he needs is sufficient funds to do so. But things are different when it comes to a T.Y. station. He may not operate a station unless some wave length is available and there are none left.
Let us now revert to clause 14 (1) of the former act which stipulated that 75 per cent of the shares were to be Canadian-owned while subclause (2) of the same clause mentioned that the owner of a T.V. station might be exempted from that requirement by order in council. The new act changes all that, as subclause (b) of clause 2 reads as follows:
b) the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to preserve ...
It says "should be effectively controlled". Now, effective control means that 51 or 52 per cent of the shares are in the hands of Canadian citizens. That means therefore, less than in

the former legislation which set the figure at 75 per cent, unless otherwise provided by order-in-council. The new legislation says "effectively controlled" but does not even mention the figure of 75 per cent any longer. The previous legislation imposed a percentage but the cabinet could turn around and favour American companies at any time. The new legislation requires only effective control that is 51 or 52 per cent but it does not even quite require that since it says "should be owned". My amendment seeks to modify the act so that it would read:
-That the Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians.
This amendment would prevent the cabinet from eluding the act as it used to do formerly and as the new legislation would still allow it to do. The new act gives even more leeway to American companies which would like to take over our television and radio stations. The 75 per cent limit is lifted. Further, the compulsory feature is removed by using the word "should" which should be replaced by "shall". The Secretary of State objects although the previous legislation said 75 per cent. The new legislation lowers the standards to an effective control which means only 51 per cent and even then, the minister does not want to be too strict since the term "should" is used. There is the Quebec television station which not only did not meet the provisions of subsection (1) of clause 141 of the previous legislation but was operating under an order in council. However, the Secretary of State says that the Quebec television station is owned by a Canadian company incorporated in Canada. It is true that the chairman is a French Canadian, a Quebecker, but he owns only one out of 10,000 shares. 50 per cent of the shares belong to Famous Players Canadian Corporation Ltd. It has been pointed out that the company is Canadian, but nevertheless, American interests hold 51.8 per cent of the shares of Famous Players Canadian Corporation Ltd. It is true that the said company is incorporated in Canada, and that the word Canada appears in its trade name, but it is controlled by American interests and the Secretary of State is aware of the fact. That company holds 50 per cent of shares of two private television stations of Quebec city and this is why I object because I would like us to have the effective control as required in the legislation and I quote:
The Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians-
January 22, 1968
If the Americans own 50 per cent of the shares, Canadians have no effective control, that is clear. I suggest we substitute to the words "should be controlled" the words "shall be controlled."
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, as I said a moment ago, airwaves are publicly owned. Wave lengths are not only limited, they are scarce. Anyone wanting to start a new television station in Quebec could not do so because there are no free wave lengths. If there are only two wave lengths available, let us not turn 50 per cent of them to the Americans but rather let us keep them for Canadians and I close by quoting the last two lines of this paragraph (b):
-and effectively controlled by Canadians so as to preserve and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada-
Do we want to enrich and strengthen it or not? It is said that effective control by Canadians is necessary to strengthen and enrich it yet effective control is given to the Americans. It is nonsensical, contradictory, and Canada and the present government have complained of this nonsense and these contradictions in the legislation and the facts.
Between the act and the facts, there are always good intentions but good intentions which are not reflected in reality. Now, when the Secretary of State, with all her charm and competence, tells us: Well, in order to preserve, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada, and I now quote clause 2:
It is hereby declared that
b) the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians ...
"Should" implies no compulsion; indeed not. Therefore, the wording is at variance with the facts and the facts are inconsistent with the wording. The words reflect the good intentions, the facts are always contrary to the words.
When we tell her: Do you really insist on that, do you stick to your opinion, to your objectives? Then, make the necessary decisions. That is all. But, they are afraid to make them.
It is just a matter of saying "shall" instead of "should", which is a mere statement of good intentions. Good intentions: hell is full of or paved with good intentions. In Quebec City there are two private TV stations and they are not effectively controlled by Canadians since 50 per cent of the interests are American. That is why the word "shall" should be substituted to "should".
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Why not? It must be like that? Indeed, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) introduced his bill, he did not say: The chartered banks should belong to Canadian interests in a proportion of 75 per cent. He said: This is how it shall be. It must be like this. It shall be like this. And his law was passed. The Minister of Finance had made up his mind. He did not say: It should. He said: It shall, it will be so. When the Americans decided to buy the Mercantile Bank, they did so. Later the minister came along with his act. He said: No. Chartered banks must belong in a proportion of 75 per cent to Canadian citizens. This should be the case and it is.
The Secretary of State, in the field of culture, uses the word "should". But, Mr. Chairman, why does the Secretary of State hesitate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The fact of the matter is that such is the case.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State says: Such is the case. Well, if so, let him put in the proper word. Why hesitate? But no, they do not want to add this word because they know full well that it is not so. And so, the word "should" is left in.
Continue to use "should"; keep your "should". It should be this, it should be that. But nobody does anything about it. Nobody moves. Let them continue like that, Mr. Chairman, and everything will be in a fine pickle, I can assure you.

Mr. Chairman, give me thirty seconds.
I live in the city of Quebec, and I cannot allow such things to be said because they are completely false and prejudicial to an enterprise controlled by a French Canadian and managed by a French Canadian. In fact, I would be remiss in allowing assertions as misleading and as contrary to the facts as those.
I ask the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) to show a certain sense of responsibility. No citizen, Mr. Chairman, would dare to deny that channel 4 is not essentially a Quebec and a French-Canadian station. The remarks repeated twenty times at least by the hon. member are unacceptable. Mr. Chairman, I did not plan to speak this evening, but this situation having arisen I should like to make some comments which go to the heart of this broadcasting bill No. C-163. I think they should be part of a general discussion on clause 2 and not be directed to individual clauses or subclauses.
I spoke on this bill on December 21 just prior to the adjournment for the Christmas recess. I believe I made myself clear with regard to my opposition to a determination expressed by the cabinet in this bill that community antenna television stations should come under the control of the new radio and television council which it is proposed to establish to replace the Board of Broadcast Governors. My time expired before I was able to complete some remarks I had prepared with regard to the action of the Board of Broadcast Governors in the year ending March 31, 1967, in refusing the applications of seven firms or individuals for CATV licences in Canada.
My observations at that time are to be found reported in Hansard for December 21. I was commenting in some detail on a letter dated December 13 which I had received from the Secretary of State. As I said on December 21, I had been pressing the Minister of Transport as well as the Secretary of State for a detailed explanation as to why seven applications for CATV licences had been turned down in Canada in the year ending March 31, 1967. It may interest members of the committee to know that under date of December 13 I received a very informative letter from the Secretary of State, a member of the cabinet for whom I have nothing but the highest regard and who in my opinion is a true Liberal. I have read extensively from her letter and intend to read from it again this evening. But I think members of this committee will be interested to learn that I also received a letter from the Minister of Transport dated December 20 and postmarked December 22, the day after the house rose. It may have been held up for signature or it may have been delayed in the Christmas mail. The interesting thing is this: the Secretary of State in her letter gives reasons for

There is not a single reason given in the letter from the Minister of Transport dated December 20, whereas the letter from the Secretary of State dated December 13 is full, explicit and informative as to the reasons for turning down these applications. As I explained on December 21, some of the reasons given for the refusal to grant CATV licence applications are such as those given in the cases of David R. Graham of Ottawa and Murray L. On December 21 I drew attention to the fact that the news and public affairs section of our broadcasting system continually played upon the riots and the vicious side of the race problem across the border but seldom, if ever, mentioned the many positive and creative changes which are taking place to improve race relations. You have heard Rap Brown, Stokely Carmichael and other extremist negro leaders interviewed over C.B.C. Why have we not heard the moderate majority leaders?

T.V. news on January 8, during the main newscast at 11 p.m., not only televised a story on the election of the first negro mayor of the city of Cleveland, Ohio, but also presented part of a talk given by the great moderate negro leader Roy Wilkins. Let me quote from an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of January 10, 1968 as follows:
The Viet Cong greatly increased their program of terror against the civilian population of South Viet Nam during 1967, with figures of murders and kidnappings rising steadily as the year progressed ... A total of 3,820 civilians were murdered by the Viet Cong during the year, compared to 1,618 killed during the previous year. But when it comes to 3,280 non-combatant men, women and children in the villages murdered deliberately in cold blood by the Viet Cong in a tragic and completely uncivilized campaign of terror, against all the rules of modern warfare as accepted by civilized countries today, we have nothing but silence from the C.B.C. news and public affairs programs.

Let me continue. There are no special programs here such as we have about every other horror front. We Canadians are being short changed by our broadcasting medium. We are not getting a true picture of this tragic war which everyone of any stature on our delegation to the I.C.C. who has spent time in Viet Nam will tell you was started, planned and directed from the beginning by North Viet Nam, as it still is. Our new bill must ensure that this kind of news censorship is not continued in the future.
When I spoke in this house before Christmas I drew to the hon. members' attention a flagrant abuse of news about the United States and a glaring anti-American bias of the public affairs and news production staff of the C.B.C. Even though there has been some improvement, there continue to be glaring examples of anti-Americanism, instead of straightforward and informative newscasting where required.
I wish to cite the following examples, since not only must the bill ensure that the C.B.C. serves Canada effectively in this field but it is vital that the newly appointed heads of the C.B.C. be informed of some of the abuses of that organization and have a more clear idea of what is ahead of them. As elected representatives of the Canadian people charged with the final responsibility for Canadian broadcasting, we have in front of us a task from which none of us may shrink.
How dangerous some reporting can be is best illustrated by an extensive year-end report given over the C.B.C. on January 2 when the C.B.C.'s Washington correspondent, Knowlton Nash, the apparent successor of the fabled anti-American James M. Minifie, told Canadians in no uncertain terms what to expect in the United States in 1968.
Nash was chairing a group of C.B.C. correspondents from all over the world. Each of them gave an opinion with regard to the area
January 22, 1968

of the world he knew best and spoke of what to expect in the coming year. Most were reasonably objective, but not so Mr. Nash with regard to the all important area of the United States, our neighbour and ally. What was shocking were the categorical statements he made on what to expect in the United States this year. He either made a direct statement or carefully selected a quote which supported his obvious anti-United States bias. The following are some of the statements made by Nash. Throughout the hour long session he repeated over and over again the following words on any excuse: "American escalation in Viet Nam", seeming to place all the world's ills here and also seeming to play the old advertising trick of scaring the public through repetition. This is not reporting, it is propaganda.
He said:
10,000 more U.S. soldiers will be killed ... the American escalation will increase in 1968 ... and they will cross into Cambodia.
He went on to make the following statements:
More and more race riots.
There will be a huge advance in the gross national product and large steps made in the race to the moon.
A growing suspicion of all governments.
A fast growing spread of the new morality.
President Johnson so unpopular that he can be beaten by anyone of the five key Republican candidates.
I should like hon. members to match Nash's categorical reporting on President Johnson's chances of re-election against the statements appearing in the Globe and Mail the very next morning. First, there was the New York Times service report from Washington which stated:
Governor Nelson A. Rockefeller of New York is the only major Republican presidential possibility who would defeat President Johnson if the 1938 election were held today, a national political survey indicates.
Why did Knowlton Nash neglect this important survey when he made his statement about all five candidates easily defeating President Johnson?
Then again, the editorial in the same paper on the same day, January 3, went even further in commenting about President Johnson:
He begins the election year with the cheering news from the Gallup poll that 46 per cent of American adults approve of the way he is handling his job ... 8 per cent more than in September and October after the summer time riots.

After noting the difficulties under which the President is labouring, the editorial continues:
Yet he may still win the nomination and the November elections. This, partly, is because a president has the priceless advantage of daily initiative in executive action as well as the semisacrosanct aura of holding in trust the nation's highest office.
How much more realistic is this assessment than Mr. Nash's bombastic attacks on the President in what can only be judged to be a deliberate policy on his part.
While speaking of President Johnson, I wonder if hon. members noted the discrepancy between what President Johnson stressed in his annual state of the union message which C.B.C. kindly carried and the C.B.C. news reporting the next morning in the important 8 a.m. newscast. The newscaster read only one long quote from the President's address in which he mentioned the seriousness of the problems facing the United States on the domestic front and the danger the nation confronted if they were not solved. He was followed by a Washington newscaster who stated that most observers felt that President Johnson's address was not only dull but it failed to provide any real program to meet the domestic crisis. He stated that most Republicans opposed his speech, and most Democrats said it was lacklustre.
In grave contrast was what the Canadian newspapers wrote the next morning. The Montreal Gazette of January 18 wrote in heavy black headlines across the top of page one: "LBJ asks for increases in taxes, jobs, housing". The sub heading read:	"Cures
outlined for domestic troubles". The paper then went on to list the vast new expenditures asked for by the president for many programs including a new government industry partnership program for training and employing the hard core unemployed; a ten year housing program for six million new dwellings; $1 billion for a model cities program; a vast new child health program; and the appointment of a special consumers council. None of these was mentioned on this key C.B.C. news program. There was only an accumulation of negatives.
Let us examine the large three-column heading in the Globe and Mail of the same morning which read: "Record Outlay, Housing Drive, Johnson's Aim". The story written

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting by Fraser Robertson from Washington starts as follows:
Focussing on the domestic scene... president Johnson last night proposed new measures to provide jobs for 500,000 hard core unemployed during the next three years, and to launch a tenfold increase over the next decade in housing construction for low income families.
While the C.B.C. tried to give the impression that the President's program was poorly received and was dull, the Ottawa Citizen in a front page story the next day wrote:
President Johnson was applauded time and again in the crowded house of representatives chamber.
Anyone listening to the address could not help but be impressed by the very loud and lengthy ovation punctuated by cheers which greeted the President when he entered the house of representatives. There are within the C.B.C. at least a few people who are either trying to foist their own anti-United States views on Canadians or are deliberately trying to stir up bad relations between the United States and Canada for reasons one can only believe are against the best interests of Canada. One observer has suggested that these people also have in mind the large listening audience along the United States border and are trying to influence them against their government's policies. This is a dangerous game if such is the case. If these charges are not accurate, we have a hopelessly incompetent news and public affairs management within the C.B.C. for which the nation is paying a fantastic bill. I wish to absolve, of course, the many honest reporters within the organization who are trying to do a job. But let us remember Tom Gould, to whom I referred on December 21, and his reasons for resigning.
Perhaps the editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of the same day reflects more appropriately the importance of the President's speech in the following comment:
What President Johnson does to combat internal U.S. problems has an importance of its own, for on it depends the future well being of the leading non-communist country of the world ... thanks to its initial idealism, its tremendous vitality, its technological prowess, its huge resources and its determined spirit, the U.S. has been able to attain a prosperity unparalleled in world history.
But it is still beset with harsh internal problems ... to a lesser extent Canadians share the same prosperity and many of the same problems. It is important to recognize the challenge, otherwise there is the danger of our affluent society becoming a complacent society that could ultimately corrode from within.

Then, again, on the 11 p.m. C.B.C. television news, following the announcement in Washington of the new and far reaching tight money policy, our C.B.C. Washington reporter Knowlton Nash commented with great certainty, as usual, that Canada would certainly be hard hit by these new United States regulations. He gave us a tear-jerker reference to the terrible fact that Canada's economy is so tightly tied to the success of the United States economy. However, within a few hours Canada's Minister of Finance stated publicly that there was every indication the United States action would not have a serious effect on Canada's economy.
One of the major methods by which Canadians are misled in C.B.C. news and public affairs reporting is by the careful omission of important stories that tend to counteract some of the favourite themes of this inner circle of united minds. For example, the Montreal Gazette of January 16 contained an article which read in part as follows:
British foreign minister George Brown-
He was speaking in Tokyo.
-yesterday praised President Johnson for going as far as you can go toward ending the war in Viet Nam and criticized North Viet Nam for refusing to do its part.
Walter Cronkite, on an American national newscast, on January 8 said:
The latest poll indicates President Johnson can win the next election handily.
On the same newscast a major story quoted George Romney, Governor of Michigan and United States presidential candidate, as saying after his return from a recent tour of Viet Nam:
The United States should not stop bombing North Viet Nam unless there is a satisfactory guarantee from North Viet Nam.
Was that before he was brainwashed or after?

Canadians will recall the extensive coverage C.B.C. gave to the famous statement Governor Romney was alleged to have made, that he was brainwashed by the army on a previous trip to Viet Nam. Why have we not heard the important follow-up by Mr. Romney? Are Canadians not supposed to hear news like that? Why have we not heard over C.B.C. a rundown of the findings of a group of 14 top United States Asian scholars?

The moderate segment of the academic community must now be heard lest other voices be mistaken for majority sentiment.
Again I would ask the question-

He does not know the answer.
