speechtext: As I said a minute ago, Mr. Chairman, I am talking about the broadcasting policy for Canada. I cannot think of a single thing that is more important than to have fair, unbiased programs in which both points of view are put before the Canadian public. If there is anything more important than that, I would like to have it pointed out tonight. This is exactly the point I am making. I submit that my time is not yet expired, and what I am now talking about is the fact that we do not have fair and unbiased programs in Canada.
Read on. Who wrote the speech?
Lubor Zink.

Then again, I ask the question, as has one other member, why, on Christmas day, should Canadians have to be subjected over C.B.C. television to a much heralded peace program starring a Canadian 27053-3681
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting interviewer, Neil Morrison, purporting to ask innocent questions of a panel of speakers at a peace conference in Switzerland? The conference speakers were composed entirely, as far as could be seen, of men well known for their opposition to United States policy in Viet Nam. It was so one-sided that even the C.B.C. announcer ended the show by saying, "You may have felt that this program was too anti-American."
Was Pope John XXIII one of those fellows?

Mr. Chairman, my time
expired when I was commenting on the seventh application for a C.A.T.V. installation that had been turned down by the board of broadcast governors, as outlined in the informative letter to me from the Secretary of State dated December 13. I have stated that the paragraph in question was full of fine-sounding phrases, but it is unfortunate that not all the facts behind the paragraph were actually placed in the letter. I have not any doubt that the paragraph in the letter is the information received from the Board of Broadcast Governors or from the Department of Transport with regard to that refusal of a CATV application for Wawa, wishing to drop the reception of the station at Sault Ste. Marie.
I should like to refer the committee to the letter received from the Minister of Transport under date December 20 in connection with this turning down of a CATV application for Wawa. The application, dated June 24, 1966, was submitted by Northern Telephone Limited, licensee of a CATV system at Montreal River, Ontario, serving Wawa, Ontario, for authority to discontinue reception from station CJIC-TV Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario and to add reception and distribution of station WWTV-TV, Cadillac, Traverse City, Michigan. Wawa is located within the proposed grade B contour of a television rebroadcasting station which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was authorized to establish at Wawa, Ontario on September 22, 1966. This station, CBLAT-3, was authorized
January 22, 1968

to commence scheduled broadcasting on December 8, 1967.
It seemed impossible to me to believe that the CATV station in operation at Wawa, Ontario proposed to drop reception from the Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario station because there is a requirement in the Radio Act that CATV stations must pick up the local T.V. station the moment they go into operation and must keep it on their dial.
In this connection I refer to numerous comments which have been made throughout the nation and in this House of Commons from time to time to the effect that CATV installations jeopardize the reception of local T.V. stations in homes in the vicinity. The statement that they jeopardize the reception of local stations is false, Mr. Chairman, because it is a requirement that CATV stations must carry on their dial the local T.V. stations.
Many people, of course, will not view programs from local T.V. stations that are on their CATV dial when there is a choice of stations. However, many people do state that CATV operators jeopardize the local T.V. stations once their installations commence operation.
In this connection I should like to read a statement made by Mr. K. J. Easton, secretary of the National Community Antenna Television Association of Canada, in a letter written from 130 Bloor street west, Toronto, and dated December 15, 1967, five weeks ago:
There appears to be some misunderstanding in Ottawa concerning the possibility that CATV operators might jeopardize the interests of a local T.V. broadcaster by removing his signal from the cable and substituting some other program material. I think this could be corrected by consideration of the following facts.
That is, the misunderstanding could be corrected.
First of course, an operator is expressly forbidden to do this by the terms of his license issued under the Radio Act and it is assumed that a similar regulation will be made by the C.R.C. under the new Broadcasting Act. The general radio regulations, part II, section 68C (1) (b) says as a condition of the license that "during the scheduled hours of operation of a station performing a Commercial Broadcasting Receiving Service, broadcasting received by that station shall not be altered or curtailed in any way except by agreement with the broadcasting station."
However, assume that an operator is prepared to contravene the conditions of his license, what is the technical possibility of his being able to prevent subscribers from receiving the local station?
It is common knowledge in the CATV industry that the weakest link in the whole system as far as susceptibility to external interference is concerned is the subscriber's television receiver and when the local T.V. transmitter is broadcasting within a few miles of the receiver, sufficient signal is picked up on the set itself to produce a strong
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting picture often equivalent to that which could be received on rabbit ears or a similar local antenna. If now a CATV cable is connected to the receiver and the signals of the local station are distributed over the cable on the same channel on which they are broadcast, then due to transmission time delay on the cable, a second image will be produced on the screen displaced from the first one and producing the effect of a heavy ghost. Generally the amount of signal picked up direct on the set is sufficient to make the resultant picture quite unacceptable.
For this reason it is the normal practice to convert the local station to some other VHF channel for distribution on the cable and not to use the local channel allocation for video program distribution at all.
Thus for example on the cable system in Ottawa, CBOT broadcasting on channel 4 is converted to channel 2 on cable, CBOFT broadcasting on channel 9 is converted to 3, and CJOH broadcasting on channel 13 is converted to 6.
Now suppose as has been implied that the CATV operator wanted to remove the local station, for example CBOFT, and replace it with another program he considers would be more acceptable to his subscribers or commercially more advantageous to him, he would have to remove it from channel 3 on the cable. However CBOFT is still receivable by the subscriber on channel 9 position on his dial because the set is picking it up direct and since there is no program on this channel on the cable, the picture will not be degraded beyond any degradation due to direct pickup at that location such as might be experienced if the set owner were not a cable subscriber.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
These facts refer to the station in Wawa where, we are told, the local CATV operator wanted to drop the Sault Ste Marie station and bring in Cadillac.
I wish to explain here that in December the C.B.C. began operating a rebroadcasting station in Wawa, Ontario, which brings in the same programs to Wawa as the local CATV operator had been bringing from Sault Ste Marie for some years past. I presume that the members of the house will be interested to learn that the programs the CATV operator in Wawa has been bringing in from Sault Ste Marie, in English only over the years, are now available in French and English over the C.B.C. rebroadcasting station which has been put into Wawa. You have the choice in Wawa, today, of getting the same program in English only, from Sault Ste Marie, through the CATV operator, or you can get the same program in English or French from the rebroadcasting station that has been established in Wawa.
Bear in mind that the CATV operator has to carry the local station. So, in Wawa, he is picking up the French and English station. I presume that there are people in this house who will say that because a program is coming in in French and English it is much
5832	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting superior to the one that is coming in in English only. But, they must realize that the operator in Wawa has two positions on his dial, one of which is taken up by the program in English entirely, and the second position which is taken up by the same program coming in in English and in French.
The operator wanted to drop the program that was coming in in English only from Sault Ste Marie, and bring in a variation-bring in the programs from Cadillac and Traverse City, Michigan. That way the people in Wawa would have a choice between the local C.B.C. station broadcasting in French and English, which is available on the CATV dial, or the Marquette, Michigan, station, or the Cadillac-Traverse City, Michigan, station.
But what happened? The Board of Broadcast Governors recommended against any such thing as dropping that Sault Ste Marie program, which they had been bringing in at great expense over the years. When I speak of "great expense over the years" I want to read into the record the correspondence that this local CATV operator has been faced with. One has to admire him for bringing in programs to the people in Wawa, and Wawa is certainly an isolated community, about 160 miles north of Sault Ste Marie.
I want you to be happy in the knowledge that the Board of Broadcast Governors has recommended to the Department of Transport, and the Department of Transport has been kind enough to accept their recommendation. Now the people at Wawa can look at the same program in English only from Sault Ste Marie or they can switch over and get the same program in English or French from the C.B.C. rebroadcast station in Wawa. Why in the name of heaven the CATV operator has to carry two similar programs on two channels on his dial I do not know, and I do not think anybody on the Board of Broadcast Governors can explain that satisfactorily.
To show you how much money the CATV operator has expended in Wawa and the efforts he has made to bring enlightenment, information and entertainment, to quote a phrase from the white paper, to the residents around Wawa, I shall read to the committee a letter, under date of December 5, 1966, written to Dr. Andrew Stewart, Chairman, Board of Broadcast Governors, 48 Kideau Street, Ottawa, Ontario:
These problems have arisen as a result of the announced intention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to establish a rebroadcasting station in Wawa, Ontario, which we understand will soon become operational.

DEBATES	January 22, 1968
It became operational within one year of this letter:
Since we are at the present time, and have been, for the past two years, providing to our subscribers in Wawa, programmes from station CJIC-TV, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario via microwave facilities leased from Northern Telephone Limited, you will readily appreciate that upon the establishment of the CBC rebroadcasting station, the residents of Wawa will find little if any need for our services since CJIC-TV is a CBC affiliate and during prime viewing times, programmes will be duplicated.
Our company is therefore faced with the prospect of abandoning its operation in the town of Wawa, and in relation to the size of the community, having to absorb the loss of a significant residual investment.
We pioneered the introduction of television in Wawa in 1958, and were responsible for fulfilling a very real need for television entertainment in this remote community.
At the outset, we brought to the residents of Wawa, one channel only, being that of the Marquette, Michigan station received off air from across Lake Superior. However, the unreliability and dubious quality of this station, received at a distance of more than 125 miles from its originating point over a large body of water, made it mandatory for our company to provide alternative programmes. Thus from the latter part of 1959 and up until November of 1964, we made available to our subscribers a second channel, consisting of films and documentaries from the National Film Board, originating from our studios.
The demands placed upon us by the residents of Wawa for Canadian programmes (hockey and football were not the least of their motives) became so great in the year 1964, that we decided to abandon the programmes of films originated from our studios and outlay the funds required to bring to Wawa, programmes from station CJIC-Sault Ste. Marie via microwave facilities leased from Northern Telephone Limited. Our lease with Northern Telephone became effective on November 27th, 1964, and is for a term of five years. Under this lease, we paid an installation charge of $12,000 and undertook to pay a yearly rental charge of $11,400 for the initial five year term.
Since the programmes of CJIC presently being carried over the microwave facilities will be of no value to our subscribers when the CBC establishes its rebroadcasting station in Wawa, Northern Telephone Limited have sought authority from the Department of Transport to substitute their present authority to carry CJIC-TV over its microwave facilities, for station WWTV-TV Cadillac, Michigan, and the authority sought by Northern Telephone is to become effective only upon the establishment by the CBC of its rebroadcasting station in Wawa.
Should such authority be granted, our company would then hope to be able to continue to subsist in Wawa, by continuing to make available to our subscribers, signals from Marquette, Michigan (albeit unreliable and of dubious value) and a stable signal from WWTV-TV Cadillac transported over Northern's existing microwave facilities.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION OF HOSPITAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think about a month ago I asked on orders of the day the following question, to be found on page 4876 of Hansard:
Can the minister say whether a decision has been made in respect of the recommendations of the Gill committee for the inclusion of hospital employees under unemployment insurance?
To that the minister replied:
-I do not think it is necessary to implement any of the recommendations of the Gill committee in order to provide coverage for hospital employees. It is now open to hospitals to apply to the commission for coverage. Employees in several hospitals are covered.
My purpose in taking advantage of this late evening period is to reiterate that question. I am sure that what the minister said was quite correct. I think he did not say quite enough, and in line with this opinion I should like to quote from a letter which I received from the unemployment insurance commissioner just a day before I asked the question. The commissioner, Mr. Hay, wrote to me as follows on November 27, 1967:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
This will acknowledge your letter addressed to the Chief Commissioner inquiring whether hospital employees are to be covered by unemployment insurance. As Mr. Laval Fortier is no longer with this Commission your letter has come to me for attention.
When the Gill Committee reviewed the Unemployment Insurance Act some time ago, it recommended that coverage be extended to hospital employees in addition to several other groups not then covered by the Act. Extension of coverage to hospital employees has also been recommended by the Unemployment Insurance Advisory Committee and by this Commission.
No decision has been announced by the Government as to what action it proposes to take regarding these recommendations. However, it has announced, as you know, that it intends to bring in certain amendments in the near future.
It is my understanding that the government is giving consideration-or was at the time I asked my question-to several amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act but that it
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion does not wish to make a change in the situation affecting hospital employees in this connection until it has an overall policy to announce; it does not want to change one part of the picture before considering the picture as a whole. If this is the case, I can understand it, but I should like to take the opportunity tonight to raise once again the question of the provisions of the act as they refer to hospital employees in the light of the recommendation of the Gill committee, the unemployment insurance advisory committee and the commission itself. I should like, if possible, to receive an answer from the government on this point.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Mackasey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION OF HOSPITAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
The hon.
member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) has accurately set out the position of hospital employees and their coverage by unemployment insurance.
It is true that the Gill report recommended to the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commissioners that coverage be extended to hospital employees. This is the case. Certainly this has been requested by both employers and employees. I understand that the reason for exempting hospital employees at the beginning was that years ago, in certain parts of the country at least, hospitals were for the most part run by charitable organizations or religious communities and it was felt that coverage of hospital employees would impose a difficult financial burden upon the organizations which made many of these hospitals possible.
I agree with the broad principle expressed by the hon. member, namely that it is desirable to adopt as soon as possible many of the recommendations of the Gill report. I think, for instance, of the fact that the Kennedy round which has recently been concluded has placed a lot of emphasis upon what the government intends to do for industry and not very much emphasis upon what the government will do for the workers of this country who could be temporarily unemployed in consequence of the dislocation which is bound to be caused during the transition period.
So, I am rather pleased to note on today's order paper, and I bring this to the attention of the hon. member, a government notice of motion in the name of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), which reads:
That the house do go Into committee of the whole at its next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution which has been recommended to the house by His Excellency:-
January 22, 1968
5834	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the coverage provided by the act; to establish a new schedule of contributions to be paid by employers on behalf of employees covered by the act; and to establish a new schedule of benefits corresponding to the new schedule of contributions.
Not being a member of the cabinet I have not seen what is proposed in detail, but from the previous statements of the minister, as

well as from the letter which the hon. gentleman was so kind to read, I would presume that in all probability this resolution will meet the problem which has been so eloquently raised by the hon. gentleman this evening.
